beats.narration_text: Hi. Can AI-generated survey data actually pass for human?

props.command: claude "test whether an AI-generated synthetic survey dataset actually matches real human personality structure"

beats.role_note: MANDATORY — BrutalistHesitantWriter, executive summary, hesitation = the pedagogy
beats.narration_text: Here's the idea. AI can generate fake survey-takers with personality scores that each look believable on their own. That sounds like enough to trust them. It isn't — because looking believable trait by trait and matching how a real personality actually holds together are two different things.

props.text:
AI can fake a survey-taker's personality scores.
If each score looks believable, that is good enough.
But believable scores can still be structurally fake.

qc.sparse_reason: hesitant-writer typing bookend accumulates one line token by token — mid-beat frames are mostly cream by design (documented exemption case in final_frame_check.py)

beats.act: CONCEPT — what a personality trait score actually is
beats.role_note: vox-style illustration (C2/C3), NOT a build-loop beat. FIXED: removed stale sparse_by_design flag now that real content is rendered.
beats.narration_text: Every synthetic respondent gets five personality numbers — the Big Five: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism. On their own, five numbers are easy to fake convincingly. The real test is whether they relate to each other the way real personalities do — whether someone scored as more anxious also tends to score as less outgoing, the way actual people do.
beats.visual_intent: five labeled dots (Manim), each glowing plausible on its own; a faint web of connecting lines appears between them, hinting the relationships are the real subject

beats.act: THE RISK — structurally fake vs individually plausible
beats.visual_intent: split screen: left — a clean reference web of correlations (real human data); right — the same five dots, individually normal-looking, but the connecting web is visibly distorted (one relationship flattened out)
beats.narration_text: Here's what that failure looks like. On the left, how the five traits actually relate to each other in real people. On the right, a synthetic set where every single trait score is fine — but one relationship between traits has quietly gone flat. Nothing about any single number would tell you that. Only checking the structure would.

lines: Every trait score looks fine on its own.
No single number would tell you that.

beats.act: THE PIPELINE — how the check actually works
beats.role_note: SourceFlow-style diagram beat. FIXED: removed stale sparse_by_design flag now that real content is rendered.
beats.narration_text: So the check runs in four steps. First, a similarity score — a Tucker's congruence coefficient — comparing the two structures directly. Second, a Jennrich test, asking whether the two are statistically different, not just visually close. Third, a bootstrap — resampling the smaller synthetic set thousands of times, so the confidence interval isn't a lie built on one lucky draw. And fourth, a per-trait distribution check, as a simpler backup signal.
beats.visual_intent: four-stage flow diagram: [Real data + Synthetic data] → [Congruence coefficient] → [Jennrich significance test] → [Bootstrap CI] → [Per-trait KS check] → [Verdict]

beats.act: VERDICT ARTIFACT — real human data vs a self-built stand-in
beats.role_note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: UI appears because the interface IS the subject here. FIXED: removed stale sparse_by_design flag now that real content is rendered.
beats.narration_text: Real output from a specific synthetic-persona tool wasn't available for this check, so first the test proves itself: against a synthetic set built to match the real structure, it passes. Against one deliberately broken in one place, it fails, correctly. That's not a verdict on any specific tool yet — it's proof the check itself catches what it's supposed to catch.
beats.visual_intent: verdict artifact page: two result cards side by side — PASS (built-to-match set) and FAIL (deliberately broken set) — each showing the congruence score, Jennrich result, and CI, captioned clearly as a self-built test case, not real tool output

beats.role_note: honest status beat — this week's real progress and blocker. FIXED: removed stale sparse_by_design flag now that real content is rendered.
beats.narration_text: The real next step is getting an actual tool's real output to run this against, instead of a stand-in. That search hit a wall this week — the real data wasn't published where it was supposed to be. The fallback is regenerating it from scratch, following the same method the tool's own documentation describes. That regeneration is in progress, and it's not finished yet.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — ClaudeComposerAsk, greeting fixed to 'Your turn.', prompt read and discussed aloud. FIXED: added folderLabel override.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you're building or testing anything with AI-generated stand-ins for real data — survey responses, user profiles, anything with structure between its parts — don't just check that each piece looks plausible. Ask Claude to check whether the relationships hold up too. Here's a prompt to start with: run a similarity check, a significance test, and a distribution check comparing your synthetic dataset's structure against your real dataset's. Paste it in and see what it finds.

props.command:
claude "compare my synthetic dataset's correlation structure
against my real dataset's — run a similarity score,
a significance test, a bootstrap confidence interval,
and a per-feature distribution check"
